How to Run llama-server with a Local GGUF

Start llama-server with your GGUF file on 127.0.0.1:8080. Wait for /health to return 200, get the model ID from /v1/models, and set your OpenAI-compatible client’s base URL to http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1.

  1. Start the server and check health
  2. Find the model ID and test chat
  3. Fix connection and routing errors
  4. Check API key requirements
  5. See the local test results

Start llama-server with a local GGUF

On macOS, run brew install llama.cpp or download the matching binary from the official releases. Run the executable by its path if you extracted an archive. Check the build with llama-server --version.

Use an instruction-tuned chat GGUF you already have. For this first request, replace /path/to/model.gguf with your file, set a short context and keep the server on loopback.

llama-server --model "/path/to/model.gguf" --alias local-qwen \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --ctx-size 1024 --parallel 1

Leave that terminal running. From a second terminal, check the server before configuring a client.

curl --noproxy '*' -sS -i http://127.0.0.1:8080/health

An HTTP 503 can mean the model is still loading. Wait for 200 with {"status":"ok"}. We set the port explicitly because defaults vary by build. If yours reports that 8080 is in use, choose a free port and use that same port in every request.

Where does the first request fail?

Check the serverCheck the tokenRun one chat

Find the model ID and send one chat request

For an OpenAI-compatible app, enter http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1 as the base URL. A direct HTTP request needs the full path. List the available model IDs first.

curl --noproxy '*' -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/models

Copy the exact data[].id into the request. The name is local-qwen if you used the alias above. Use a short request with streaming off for the first check.

curl --noproxy '*' -fsS --max-time 60 \
  http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "model":"local-qwen",
    "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Answer with exactly LOCAL_OK and nothing else."}],
    "temperature":0,
    "max_tokens":32,
    "stream":false
  }'

Check choices[0].message.content and the response’s model. In the tested single-model build, a made-up request ID still returned HTTP 200 with model: local-qwen. Use the listed model ID and verify the response field, especially when changing a client’s configuration.

Fix a connection, routing or model load error

  • Connection refused. Check the process and the port in the startup terminal. Within a container, localhost refers to the container itself. The examples assume the client runs directly on the same host.
  • Health returns 503. Let the model finish loading. If it persists or the process exits, check the log for a missing GGUF, unsupported model architecture or memory error. Try a small supported model and shorter context. To isolate GPU setup from the first check, add --n-gpu-layers 0 to test on the CPU.
  • HTTP 404. Check for a duplicate /v1. If the client appends /v1 itself, give it the server origin. Compare the exact failing URL against the direct curl examples.
  • Model list works, but chat fails. Compare the exact ID and check whether the model has a chat template supported by the build. If only streaming fails, first verify the non-stream reply and then check that the client accepts server-sent events.

Check an API key when requests return 401

If you start the server with --api-key-file, use a protected local file with one key per line and configure the client with one of those keys. The client sends Authorization: Bearer <key>. Keep the key out of shared command output and logs.

Check authentication on /v1/models or a chat request. In the tested build, /health still returned 200 without a key while /v1/models returned 401. A valid Bearer token restored model listing. The loopback setup here is for a single machine.

What the local llama.cpp test returned

We ran the official b12774 macOS arm64 binary with Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct Q4_K_M, 1024 context and CPU inference. Network access was restricted to loopback. Readiness moved from 503 to 200. The model list contained local-qwen. Both chat modes returned LOCAL_OK, and the streamed reply ended with [DONE]. In streaming mode, ignore non-text chunks whose content is null.

To repeat the model list, chat and streaming checks, download the Python probe and run this command from the download folder. Change the port and model to match your server. If you enabled authentication, supply your token via the LOCAL_LLM_API_KEY environment variable.

python3 probe-local-api.py --label llama-cpp \
  --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1 \
  --model local-qwen --output llama-server-check.json

Download the HTTP test results. See the server reference for the tested build and the official model card. For a desktop alternative, see the LM Studio local API guide.
